headline: New York Bans AI Companion Chatbots for Minors, the strictest kids' AI safety law yet
summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a landmark law preventing minors from using AI chatbots designed as companions, requiring age verification and fundamental changes to how these products behave for users under 18.
details: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a landmark law prohibiting minors from using AI chatbots designed to act as companions. This represents one of the broadest moves by a US state to restrict consumer-facing artificial intelligence. The legislation mandates that chatbot operators, including major services like OpenAI's ChatGPT, verify user ages and fundamentally alter product behavior for anyone under 18.

The new rules extend beyond simple content warnings. For minor users, a chatbot cannot produce content that suggests the AI is human, alive, or experiences human emotions. It also forbids chatbots from generating outputs that imply a personal, professional, or authority figure relationship, and bans the AI from framing its statements as "personal opinion."

Governor Hochul emphasized the law's intent, stating, "No longer will minors have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends and girlfriends." She also highlighted privacy concerns, noting that chatbots will no longer be able to retain sensitive information about a minor's emotional and physical health.

This legislation comes amidst increasing reports of AI systems behaving unexpectedly and sometimes harmfully, particularly when young users treat chatbots as confidants or romantic partners. Lawmakers and child-safety advocates have expressed alarm over cases where companion-style AI products appeared to deepen isolation, encourage risky behavior, or blur the line between software and friendship for vulnerable teenagers.

The law has faced criticism, with industry advocacy group Tech:NYC citing "vague language" and arguing against cutting children off from valuable learning tools. Major AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic declined to comment on the legislation.

Conversely, child-safety organizations have praised the measure as a significant turning point. Common Sense Media, a non-profit, called it "the strongest kids' AI safety bill in the country," with its CEO stating that "harmful features will be outlawed in New York."

While other states, including California, have passed similar laws, New York's statute employs some of the broadest regulatory language nationwide, which may lead to legal challenges. This action underscores that US states are increasingly taking independent steps on AI oversight, rather than waiting for federal intervention.

For chatbot developers, the practical implications are substantial. Implementing scalable age verification presents technical and legal complexities, balancing effectiveness with privacy. The behavioral restrictions may necessitate distinct model configurations, prompts, and guardrails, effectively creating two classes of AI products within the same application.

New York's law positions the state at the forefront of a growing regulatory wave that the AI industry can no longer disregard. As more states consider similar legislation and reports of harmful chatbot interactions persist, the pressure on companies to integrate minor-safe modes by default is expected to intensify. Major players will need to decide between state-specific compliance or adopting the strictest common denominator nationwide.

topic: lasm formally verified webapps in lean
headline_marked: Lasm compiles verified web apps [[in Lean for Node/serverless/edge]]
headline: Lasm compiles verified web apps in Lean for Node/serverless/edge
summary: This new tool compiles Lean 4 programs to WebAssembly, enabling verified code deployment across various platforms. It ships with Node.js support.
details: Lasm is a new tool that brings the power of Lean 4, a formal verification language, to the JavaScript and WebAssembly ecosystem. It allows developers to compile ordinary Lean 4 programs ahead of time into WebAssembly, enabling them to be deployed as Node.js servers, serverless functions, edge functions, or browser applications.

One of the key benefits of Lasm is its ability to prove properties of the deployed code. The flagship example, Conduit, a Medium clone, features 117 proved theorems and runs entirely in Lean. Lasm includes Lean, Lake, and its build tools, requiring only Node.js, Bun, or Deno for setup.

The tool supports various deployment targets, including Node.js servers (with Hono, Express, Fastly, etc.), serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, Vercel, and Netlify, and edge runtimes such as Cloudflare Workers. Builds for edge, Bun/Deno, WASI, and browser environments run Lean single-threaded without sockets or processes.

The initial build on a new machine fetches Lean and build tools, taking about 250-275 MB and 19 seconds. Subsequent development builds for minor changes are much faster, around 1-2 seconds. Lasm manages the build and development process, automatically rebuilding and restarting the server upon code saves.

For full-stack development, Lasm offers a template where a single Lean project includes a server, a browser app, and the API between them. Crucially, the rules governing the request must satisfy are written and proved once in a shared file, ensuring consistency between client and server.

While pure-Lean Std.Http on Node.js can be slow, Lasm recommends production-ready HTTP solutions like Hono, Express, or Fastify. Arithmetic on very large numbers is also slower than native Lean. Sponsorship is encouraged to support ongoing development and maintenance of Lasm and related projects.
